title: Binary search trees
summary: Smaller to the left, bigger to the right: search, insert and delete in O(height).

steps.title: Binary search, as a tree
body: A **binary search tree** (BST) keeps one rule at every node: everything in the **left** subtree is smaller, everything in the **right** subtree is bigger.

So searching is binary search: compare with the node, go left or right, and half of what is left is ruled out. Watch `cur` walk down to 6 in the trace. The cost is the tree's **height**: `O(log n)` when it is balanced.

public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }

steps.prompt: Search the same tree for a value that is not there. What does it print?
code: var root = new TreeNode(8, new TreeNode(3, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(6, new TreeNode(4), new TreeNode(7))), new TreeNode(10, null, new TreeNode(14)));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }
steps.explain: 5 < 8 go left, 5 > 3 go right, 5 < 6 go left, 5 > 4 go right: `null`. If 5 were inserted, that empty spot is exactly where it would go.

steps.title: Insert where the search fails
body: To insert, search for the value; the `null` where the search falls off is its place. Recursively:
else if (value > node.Value) node.Right = Insert(node.Right, value);
return node;   // equal: already present, nothing to do

`root = Insert(root, x)` works even for an empty tree. The order of inserts decides the shape: inserting `1, 2, 3, 4, 5` in order builds a chain of height 5, a linked list in disguise. Self-balancing trees (like the red-black tree inside `SortedSet<T>`) fix that automatically.

steps.prompt: Starting from an empty BST, insert `5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3`. What does an **in-order** traversal give?
steps.explain: In-order visits left, node, right, and in a BST left means smaller. So in-order always lists a BST in **sorted** order. (5 2 1 3 8 9 is the pre-order.)
Smaller values live on the left. When `node` becomes `null` the value cannot be anywhere.

steps.title: Deleting a node
body: Deleting has three cases, depending on how many children the node has:
1. **No children**: just remove it (return `null` to its parent).
2. **One child**: replace the node by that child.

3. **Two children**: find its **successor**, the smallest value in its right subtree (go right once, then left as far as possible). Copy that value into the node, then delete the successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so that delete is case 1 or 2.

prompt: You delete `8` (the root, two children) from this tree, using the successor rule. Which value replaces it?
steps.explain: The successor is found by going right to 10, then left as far as possible; 10 has no left child, so it is 10. (The mirror rule, using the largest value on the left, 7, the *predecessor*, would also keep the tree valid.)

steps.title: Insert and search
prompt: - `TreeNode Insert(TreeNode? node, int value)`: returns the (possibly new) root; inserting a value already present changes nothing.
The tests insert 100,000 values in a shuffled order, so the tree stays fairly balanced, and then search them all.
solution: else if (value > node.Value) node.Right = Insert(node.Right, value);
template: {{CODE}}
List<int> DojoInOrder(TreeNode? n) { var r = new List<int>(); void V(TreeNode? x) { if (x == null) return; V(x.Left); r.Add(x.Value); V(x.Right); } V(n); return r; }
TreeNode? dojoRoot = null;
foreach (var dojoX in new[] { 5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3, 8 }) dojoRoot = Insert(dojoRoot, dojoX);
Dojo.Eq("in-order is sorted, duplicate ignored", new List<int> { 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9 }, DojoInOrder(dojoRoot));
Dojo.Eq("the first value is the root", 5, dojoRoot!.Value);
Dojo.Eq("3 went left then right", 3, dojoRoot.Left!.Right!.Value);
Dojo.Eq("Contains(9)", true, Contains(dojoRoot, 9));
Dojo.Eq("Contains(4) is false", false, Contains(dojoRoot, 4));
Dojo.Eq("empty tree contains nothing", false, Contains(null, 1));
var dojoRng = new Random(3);
var dojoVals = Enumerable.Range(0, 100_000).Select(i => i * 2).OrderBy(_ => dojoRng.Next()).ToArray();
TreeNode? dojoBig = null;
foreach (var dojoX in dojoVals) dojoBig = Insert(dojoBig, dojoX);
Dojo.Eq("100,000 values: all even ones found", true, dojoVals.All(x => Contains(dojoBig, x)));
Dojo.Eq("100,000 values: odd ones missing", false, Enumerable.Range(0, 1000).Any(i => Contains(dojoBig, i * 2 + 1)));

steps.title: Delete
prompt: Write `TreeNode? Delete(TreeNode? node, int value)`: removes `value` if present and returns the new root of this subtree. Handle all three cases; for two children, use the **successor** (smallest value in the right subtree).
solution: if (value < node.Value) { node.Left = Delete(node.Left, value); return node; }
if (value > node.Value) { node.Right = Delete(node.Right, value); return node; }
template: {{CODE}}
List<int> DojoInOrder(TreeNode? n) { var r = new List<int>(); void V(TreeNode? x) { if (x == null) return; V(x.Left); r.Add(x.Value); V(x.Right); } V(n); return r; }
TreeNode DojoTree() => new TreeNode(8, new TreeNode(3, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(6, new TreeNode(4), new TreeNode(7))), new TreeNode(10, null, new TreeNode(14)));
Dojo.Eq("delete a leaf (7)", new List<int> { 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 14 }, DojoInOrder(Delete(DojoTree(), 7)));
var dojoA = Delete(DojoTree(), 10);
Dojo.Eq("delete a node with one child (10)", new List<int> { 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 14 }, DojoInOrder(dojoA));
Dojo.Eq("14 moved up to replace 10", 14, dojoA!.Right!.Value);
var dojoB = Delete(DojoTree(), 3);
Dojo.Eq("delete a node with two children (3)", new List<int> { 1, 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 14 }, DojoInOrder(dojoB));
Dojo.Eq("its successor 4 took its place", 4, dojoB!.Left!.Value);
var dojoC = Delete(DojoTree(), 8);
Dojo.Eq("delete the root", new List<int> { 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, 14 }, DojoInOrder(dojoC));
Dojo.Eq("the new root is 10", 10, dojoC!.Value);
Dojo.Eq("deleting a missing value changes nothing", 8, DojoInOrder(Delete(DojoTree(), 5)).Count);
Dojo.Eq("deleting the only node gives an empty tree", true, Delete(new TreeNode(1), 1) == null);
